A NASA Space Apps entry for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten"

Al Isra'a

Every mission to the Moon and Mars left something behind: landers, rovers, a family photograph, two golf balls. None of it is coming home. This page tells what each thing did and why it stayed, and shows only what NASA has formally adopted that touches it: laws, contracts and programmes. Choose an object on the globe.

Round dots are old equipment. Select one to open it. Drag to turn the globe, or use the left and right arrow keys to move between objects. The globe is a drawing, not a photograph.

What NASA's adopted plans mean for it

When each one fell silent

    What NASA has adopted

    Everything in this section is a law, a signed contract, a funded programme or a published NASA policy. Dates are NASA's targets as of November 2026 and have moved before. An estimated 500,000 pounds of human-made material sits on the Moon.

    Law and agreement

    Protecting historic sites

    NASA published guidance in 2011 on keeping clear of Apollo and other United States artifacts on the Moon, and a 2020 law builds on it. Under the Artemis Accords, signing countries state their intent to preserve historic sites and artifacts in space.

    What it means for the old equipment This is the one adopted policy written for the old equipment itself. It keeps new missions at a distance from it.

    Programme under way

    Moon Base

    NASA's Moon Base plan, released in March 2026, has three phases. Phase 1, from now to 2029, starts with up to 25 missions, including 21 landings, mostly robotic and early uncrewed.

    What it means for the old equipment It will put people on the same world as this hardware again. Nothing in the programme is aimed at the old machines.

    Schedule

    Artemis crew flights

    Artemis II took four astronauts around the Moon. Artemis III is a 2027 test in low Earth orbit with commercial landers. NASA targets an early-2028 crewed landing for Artemis IV and a late-2028 landing for Artemis V. NASA has identified nine candidate landing regions near the south pole.

    What it means for the old equipment Crews land in the south polar region, far from the Apollo and Surveyor sites. Lunar Prospector's impact site is the piece of old equipment in that region.

    Contract awarded

    Lunar relay satellites

    In 2024 NASA selected Intuitive Machines to develop the first lunar relays, which will launch in stages. They are the first implementation of LunaNet, NASA's framework for shared, internet-like links at the Moon.

    What it means for the old equipment The relays are for new missions. The only old item still working is a reflector that needs no radio at all.

    Contract awarded

    Mars Telecommunications Network

    On 1 September 2026 NASA awarded Blue Origin a contract worth up to about $700 million to deliver a high-performance Mars telecommunications orbiter by 31 December 2028.

    What it means for the old equipment It is built for future missions. The silent landers and rovers have no way to call it.

    Being redesigned

    Mars Sample Return

    NASA has announced a new approach to bringing Perseverance's samples back, and expects to confirm the programme and its design in the second half of 2026.

    What it means for the old equipment The ten tubes at Three Forks have no adopted ride home.

    Prize challenge

    LunaRecycle

    NASA's LunaRecycle Challenge, launched in 2024 with $3 million in prizes, seeks ways to recycle waste such as food packaging and discarded clothing on long missions. Its Phase 2 first prize went to an MIT team on 28 August 2026.

    What it means for the old equipment It is about not adding to the pile. It does not touch what is already there.

      Showing —.

      Where it lies

      Longitude and latitude on a flat map of each world. Dots are old equipment and diamonds are prospective base sites. The ringed dot is open beside it, and the pulsing dot still works.

      From landing to silence, and what NASA plans next

      Each bar runs from the day it reached the surface to the day it went quiet. Diamonds on the bottom lane are NASA's adopted plans. The dashed line is today.

      Prospective base sites

      On the Moon, the nine regions NASA has identified for the first Artemis crewed landing, where NASA expects to start its Moon Base. On Mars, NASA has not chosen a site, so these are five of the 47 zones proposed at NASA's 2015 human landing site workshop, chosen here because each has old NASA equipment nearby. Diamonds on the map above show them. Click a card to see its nearest old equipment.

      Close-up of the lunar south pole

      Looking down on the pole, out to 80° south. Positions of the regions are approximate.

      All nine Artemis regions sit within a few hundred kilometres of the pole, where sunlight lasts longest and shadowed craters may hold ice. The only old NASA equipment in this collection that lies nearby is Lunar Prospector, crashed on purpose into Shoemaker crater in 1999.

        How the numbers are worked out

        "Years silent" counts from the last day each object worked, or the day it was left or crashed, to today. Objects that never carried a radio count from the day they were left. The Apollo 11 reflector still works, so it has no silence. Landing dates are mission landing or impact dates. The signal button uses the real 2.6-second round trip for the Moon. A real round trip to Mars takes about 6 to 44 minutes, so it is sped up.
